newsitem.title: UK: Top futures exchanges link up ahead of single currency.
newsitem.headline: Top futures exchanges link up ahead of single currency.

text.p: Two big European futures exchanges linked up with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange Wednesday, carving up business among them ahead of the planned single European currency.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) said it signed a deal with the CME to link trading in some interest rate futures and options contracts.
The French futures and options exchange Matif signed an accord with the CME to start Matif's French bond future that will apply to all contracts of one year or more.
"We are very satisfied with this agreement which constitutes an important milestone in our committed strategy of preparation for monetary union," said Gerard Pfauwald, president of MATIF.
Financial exchanges have been jostling for position ahead of the planned launch of single European currency, to be known as the euro, in 1999.
Market participants said LIFFE's case for being a primary exchange for euro contracts would be strengthened by a link with another major exchange.
"LIFFE is trying to ensure they will be integral in a (single currency) world," said a director of a U.S. futures house in London.

A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell a commodity or financial instruments at a set price on a specific date. An option contract grants the right but not the obligation to buy or sell a stock, bond, currency or other instrument at a set price by a certain time.
The contracts are widely used by investors and corporations as tools to make money and limit risk on their other investments.

The LIFFE-CME link will start with three-month Euromark futures, under a pact where LIFFE's short-term interest rate futures and options can be traded on CME after LIFFE has closed, extending the trading day for the LIFFE contracts.

A link between LIFFE and the Chicago Board of Trade is already under development, and after an initial postponement as a result of technical difficulties, is scheduled to start next May. The exchanges said on Tuesday that the link would be amended to include trading some euro debt products in its open outcry pits.
MATIF said its agreement was initially for five years.

While the 10-year French franc bond future and options contracts will be the first to trade, MATIF products with "a maturity of more than one year, denominated in francs, Ecu, the euro, or any other European currency," are also covered.

Wigglesworth said LIFFE was in constant contact with other exchanges around the world, although he said it was not easy to establish joint-ventures with those in the same time zone without splitting liquidity.
